asks: What does Silo know about an ecosystem?
answer: Silo keeps what it knows of package ecosystems as data that ships with it, one file per ecosystem, as it keeps what it knows of each agent program; no ecosystem is named in Silo's code. For each ecosystem, such as npm, Cargo or pip, the file names the folders a rebuild brings back, such as node_modules or target, each with the files a rebuild starts from that stand beside it, such as package-lock.json or Cargo.lock; the folders where its tools keep their package caches, such as ~/.npm or ~/.cargo/registry, which those tools fill again when they are gone; and the hosts of its package registries. A folder counts as brought back by a rebuild only where one of its starting files stands beside it, and a cache only at the place its file names. A package in such a folder is only here when a rebuild would not bring it back as it is. That is the case when its starting file does not name it, such as one installed there by hand with pip (`hand-installed-package`), and when its files were changed after it was installed, such as a fix made by hand inside node_modules. How each ecosystem shows such a package is to find out, and until it is found for an ecosystem, its folders that can hold one count as only here. A test refuses a shipped file that does not match its type. A file that does not match when Silo loads it is refused, with the field at fault, and its ecosystem then counts as one the data does not know. A folder that only bears the name, and every folder of an ecosystem the data does not know, counts as only here (`what-would-bring-it-back`).
